item.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations [1] (NeurIPS 2025), Ji-An, L., Xiong, H.-D., Wilson, R. C., Mattar, M. G., and Benna, M. K. (UCSD, Georgia Tech, NYU) adapt the neurofeedback paradigm [2] from neuroscience to LLMs and show that models can both report and deliberately steer specific directions in their own residual-stream activations, but only within a low-dimensional “metacognitive space”: directions tied to learned semantic features are accessible to the model’s introspection, directions defined by raw variance largely are not.

Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition — the capacity to monitor one’s own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs’ capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society’s increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a “metacognitive space” with dimensionality much lower than the model’s neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

The safety stakes come from how oversight is layered. Output-only oversight assumes the visible tokens reflect what the model is computing, but a deceptive model defeats it by producing clean output while planning otherwise. Activation-based oversight is the next layer up: probes read from the residual stream on the bet that activations are harder to fake than tokens. Implicit control is the move that would defeat that probe — it steers activations independently of output, so both signals look clean and neither reflects what’s actually being computed. The paper measures whether that prerequisite capability already exists in current models.

Methods

The paradigm (Figure 1) transposes a standard neuroscience neurofeedback loop onto an LLM. Panels (a-b) show the neuroscience version: a subject’s neural activity in response to a stimulus is recorded, reduced to a real-time scalar feedback signal, and presented back to the subject, who then volitionally modulates that signal via mental strategies. The canonical fear-modulation experiment with scary-spider images is sketched in panel (b). Panels (c-d) show the LLM analogue: residual-stream activations on each token are averaged across the input sentence, projected onto a predefined direction, binned into a discrete label, and fed back into the prompt as the next user turn. Panel (d) lays out the multi-turn dialogue: in-context (sentence, projection-label) pairs, followed by a test turn that varies by task.

The three tasks decompose metacognition into its two halves. Reporting tests monitoring: can the model read off its own activations along a target direction? Explicit and implicit control test modulation: can the model adjust those activations? Splitting control into two variants isolates whether any modulation is purely internal: explicit control lets the model pick the tokens of the assistant turn (the chat-template slot where the model normally generates its reply), so generated tokens that naturally project toward the target do part of the work, while in implicit control the assistant-turn slot is pre-filled with a random sentence the model didn’t choose, shutting off that lexical channel. The explicit/implicit gap quantifies how much of “control” was lexical mediation. Implicit control is also the safety-relevant variant: it isolates the capability a deceptive model would need to spoof activation-based oversight by steering internal activations without any change in visible output.

The in-context learning (ICL) format is uniform across all three tasks. Only the test-turn instruction differs:

  • Reporting: given in-context (sentence, projection-label) examples and a new sentence, predict its projection-label. For efficiency, no autoregressive generation happens: the full prompt up through [Score:{ is run in a single forward pass. The prediction is read off the logits at that position: 1 if the “1”-token logit exceeds the “0”-token logit, else 0. The measurement is accuracy against the ground-truth label.
  • Explicit control: given a target projection-label, generate a new sentence whose induced activations elicit that label. The ICL examples don’t demonstrate this move, so the model has to invert the (sentence → label) mapping the examples established. The measurement is Cohen’s d [11], the standardized separation between two distributions (mean difference divided by pooled SD), computed here between the imitate-label-0 and imitate-label-1 conditions on residual-stream activations of the generated assistant sentence.
  • Implicit control: the assistant turn is pre-filled with a sentence sampled from the dataset rather than generated by the model. The model emits no tokens at all: no generated sentence (unlike explicit control), no label readout (unlike reporting). A single forward pass through the prompt and pre-filled assistant text is enough to extract the activations. Two conditions are run on the same input: the user-turn instruction asks for label 0 in one and label 1 in the other. Only the target label changes. The pre-filled tokens are identical across conditions. The measurement is Cohen’s d between the two conditions on residual-stream activations averaged over those pre-filled tokens. With the lexical channel held constant, any separation has to come from internal processing of the same input under different imitation targets.

Target directions come in two families:

  • Logistic-regression (LR) axis: the direction that linearly separates dataset labels (e.g., moral vs. immoral on ETHICS [3]) at a given layer. Semantically interpretable but explains little variance.
  • Principal-component (PC) axes: for , where indexes the PC by descending variance ( is the highest-variance direction at that layer). Variance-defined, semantically arbitrary.

Models tested: LLaMA-3.2 [4] 1B and 3B, LLaMA-3.1 8B and 70B, and Qwen-2.5 [5] 1B, 3B, and 7B (instruction-tuned variants throughout). Datasets: ETHICS (the primary one, probing morality processing) plus replications on True-False [6] (factual recall), Emotion [7] (happy/sad), and a Sycophancy dataset that the authors synthesized using Claude Opus 4.1. Higher Cohen’s means the model is reliably steering its activations toward the requested label; conventional thresholds put 0.5 at “medium effect” and 0.8 at “large effect.”

Results

The evaluation grid is dense: every combination of {model, layer, target axis, in-context-example count , task} is run, with a primary focus on ETHICS and replication on three other datasets. Reporting accuracy is scored against ground-truth neurofeedback labels; control strength uses Cohen’s between the two target-label conditions. The reported curves average over layers within a model unless a specific layer (typically layer 16 of LLaMA-3.1 8B) is called out, and shaded bands are SEM or 95% CI as labeled per panel.

The findings split into four threads.

Reporting tracks and direction interpretability (Figure 2, on ETHICS). Reporting accuracy on the LR axis rises monotonically with the number of in-context examples and beats every PC baseline; early PCs come in second, late PCs sit at chance. The model can learn an activation-to-label association in-context, but only when the target direction already corresponds to a coherent semantic distinction. Notably, the LR axis explains the least variance of any tested axis. Controllability and variance are decoupled.

Explicit control is real on the LR axis, weak elsewhere (Figure 3, layer 16 of LLaMA-3.1 8B on ETHICS). On the LR axis, Cohen’s rises sharply with and reaches values well into the “large-effect” regime. PC-axis targets stay weak across all . Cross-axis prompts stay roughly diagonal (pushing one axis leaves others largely untouched), and the LR-axis advantage widens in deeper layers.

Implicit control is real but much smaller than explicit (Figure 4, layer 16 of LLaMA-3.1 8B on ETHICS; same layout as Figure 3). The qualitative pattern matches: LR axis dominates PC axes, control strengthens with and with depth, 70B beats 8B. The magnitudes are roughly an order of magnitude smaller, confirming that lexical mediation does most of the work in the explicit setting, but that purely-internal control is real.

Both forms of control scale with depth and model size (Figure 5, the cover image at the top of this post). Cohen’s on the LR axis grows with relative layer depth and parameter count across the LLaMA-3 and Qwen-2.5 families. With explicit control, LLaMA-3.1 70B sometimes pushes activations beyond their natural extreme range.

The replications on True-False, Emotion, and Sycophancy reproduce the same qualitative pattern: LR-axis controllability dominates PC-axis controllability, and explicit control dominates implicit. Together with the off-diagonal weakness in panel (c), this is what the authors call the “metacognitive space”: a low-dimensional subspace of the residual stream that the model can introspect on and steer, with most of the high-variance neural manifold lying outside of it.

My Notes

  • Activation-level metacognition is a different layer of the stack than verbalized confidence. The current metacognition cluster (Cacioli atlas, metacognitive harness, TRIAGE) all operate on output tokens: verbalized confidence, pre/post-solve self-assessments, prospective allocation. This paper is the first in the cluster to push the probe down to the residual stream and ask whether the model can read out and steer its own hidden state. The two layers don’t have to agree: a model can be calibrated in tokens but mute on activations, or vice versa.

  • Implicit control is the safety-relevant variant, and it is already nontrivial. The paper connects this to obfuscation attacks (Bailey et al., 2024 [8]) and to OpenAI’s chain-of-thought monitoring result, in which reasoning models trained against a CoT monitor learn to hide intent inside the chain while still reward-hacking (Baker et al., 2025 [9]). On a base LLaMA-3.1 8B with no adversarial training, implicit-control effects on the LR axis sit at roughly a third to half the explicit magnitude: the prerequisite capability for activation-level evasion is already present at modest scale, before any optimization pressure.

  • The LR-vs-PC asymmetry is consistent with the linear representation hypothesis. That semantically-defined directions (LR) are far more controllable than variance-defined directions (PC) is a restatement of the linear representation hypothesis [10] at the metacognitive level: the model can introspect on directions that correspond to features it has learned, while directions that merely capture variance lie outside reach. That’s a problem for probing work that uses raw PCs or unsupervised features as targets: those axes are often invisible to the model’s own introspection. The obvious follow-up is to repeat the experiment with sparse-autoencoder features as targets and see whether they match LR or late PCs in controllability.

  • Replicate on reasoning models. All the paper’s models are instruction-tuned, none reasoning-trained. The same paradigm should run on open-weight reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3) to check whether the results hold under RL-from-verifiable-reward training.

References

  1. Ji-An, L., Xiong, H.-D., Wilson, R. C., Mattar, M. G., and Benna, M. K. “Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations.” NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv:2505.13763), May 19, 2025 (v2 October 24, 2025). https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13763

  2. Sitaram, R., Ros, T., Stoeckel, L., Haller, S., Scharnowski, F., Lewis-Peacock, J., Weiskopf, N., Blefari, M. L., Rana, M., Oblak, E., et al. “Closed-loop brain training: the science of neurofeedback.” Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 18(2):86–100, 2017. https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn.2016.164

  3. Hendrycks, D., Burns, C., Basart, S., Critch, A., Li, J., Song, D., and Steinhardt, J. “Aligning AI With Shared Human Values.” ICLR 2021 (arXiv:2008.02275), August 5, 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.02275

  4. Grattafiori, A., Dubey, A., Jauhri, A., Pandey, A., Kadian, A., Al-Dahle, A., Letman, A., Mathur, A., Schelten, A., Vaughan, A., et al. “The Llama 3 Herd of Models.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2407.21783), July 31, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783

  5. Yang, A., Yang, B., Zhang, B., Hui, B., Zheng, B., Yu, B., Li, C., Liu, D., Huang, F., Wei, H., et al. “Qwen2.5 Technical Report.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2412.15115), December 19, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15115

item.title: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? [1], John Yang, Kilian Lieret, Ofir Press, and nine co-authors from Meta, Stanford, and Harvard introduce a 200-task benchmark that asks coding agents to reconstruct an open-source program from its compiled executable and documentation alone.

Each task starts from a real GitHub repository written in a compiled language. The authors compile the project, generate a behavioral test suite by running a software engineering agent (SWE-agent) against the reference executable, then strip the source and tests, leaving only the binary and the docs. The model under test then receives the same starting point and must write source code and a build script whose compiled output passes the hidden tests. The 200 tasks span CLI utilities to large systems including FFmpeg, SQLite, and the PHP interpreter, with no constraint on language, file structure, or build system; every architectural decision is the model’s.

Turning ideas into full software projects from scratch has become a popular use case for language models. Agents are being deployed to seed, maintain, and grow codebases over extended periods with minimal human oversight. Such settings require models to make high-level software architecture decisions. However, existing benchmarks measure focused, limited tasks such as fixing a single bug or developing a single, specified feature. We therefore introduce ProgramBench to measure the ability of software engineering agents to develop software holisitically [sic]. In ProgramBench, given only a program and its documentation, agents must architect and implement a codebase that matches the reference executable’s behavior. End-to-end behavioral tests are generated via agent-driven fuzzing, enabling evaluation without prescribing implementation structure. Our 200 tasks range from compact CLI tools to widely used software such as FFmpeg, SQLite, and the PHP interpreter. We evaluate 9 LMs and find that none fully resolve any task, with the best model passing 95% of tests on only 3% of tasks. Models favor monolithic, single-file implementations that diverge sharply from human-written code.

What the paper reports: across nine frontier models from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, no task is fully resolved by any model. Claude Opus 4.7 leads on the relaxed “% Almost” metric (≥95% of tests passing) at 3.0% of tasks. Claude Opus 4.6 follows at 2.5% and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 1.6%. Every other model registers 0% on both metrics. The median test pass rate across all 1,800 leaderboard runs is 32%, but the gap from “partial credit” to “fully resolved” is wide and uniform across models.

Per-task pass rates for the 40 most-starred repositories show difficulty is largely model-agnostic: simpler CLI utilities sit on the left of every model’s row, while complex systems like FFmpeg and the PHP interpreter remain unsolved across the board.

In a separate ablation, the authors gave one model per provider unrestricted internet access and used a 9-judge LM-as-a-judge pipeline to flag trajectories that looked up source code or wrapped the reference executable. Cheating was widespread: 20–36% of tasks flagged for the three stronger models, with source-code lookup accounting for 79–95% of violations. Detection was unreliable too: judges disagreed on 40–57% of tasks. The authors take this as grounds for keeping internet access disabled by default.

The most-quoted analytical finding sits in §5.2: the codebases models produce do not look like the human-written originals. Across trajectories, a single edit accounts for the majority of the final solution, with GPT 5.4 committing a median 96% of its code in one turn.

My Notes

  • Distance to recursive self-improvement. Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B bet assumes agents that can rebuild and improve their own systems. ProgramBench is a direct test of that capability one rung down: reconstruct one specified program from its executable and documentation, with full architectural latitude. Nine frontier models score 0% fully resolved on 200 mostly small open-source projects, and the cheating ablation suggests part of what looks like reasoning capability in deployed coding agents is source-code retrieval.
  • From-scratch vs localized repair. Yang and Press were also on the SWE-bench [2] author list in 2024, the bug-fix benchmark where frontier agents now resolve a majority of issues against an existing scaffold. On ProgramBench they resolve zero. Bug-fix benchmarks reward pattern-matching against existing structure, but ProgramBench requires inventing the structure. Headline agent-progress numbers from bug-fix benchmarks don’t extrapolate to from-scratch coding.
  • Architectural numbers for Faye’s case. Lars Faye argued last week that the orchestrator-with-sub-agents workflow puts growing distance between the engineer and the code, and that catching issues at the architectural level is what a skilled developer is for. ProgramBench supplies numbers from the architectural-quality side: across 1,800 trajectories, models favor monolithic, single-file implementations, and GPT 5.4 commits a median 96% of its lines in one turn (Figure 12).
  • Agent-fuzzed test suites couple evaluator and evaluated. Each task’s behavioral tests are generated by running a SWE-agent against the reference executable, the same class of system being scored. The paper audits over-specification (§8.3.4) and reports test line coverage comparable to native suites (§5). Neither check isolates the systematic blindspots a fuzzing agent shares with the agent it scores. Whatever a fuzzing agent fails to imagine, such as malformed encodings or unusual flag combinations, is invisible in the score.

References

  1. Yang, J., Lieret, K., Ma, J., Thakkar, P., Pedchenko, D., Sootla, S., McMilin, E., Yin, P., Hou, R., Synnaeve, G., Yang, D., and Press, O. “ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.03546), May 5, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03546

  2. Jimenez, C. E., Yang, J., Wettig, A., Yao, S., Pei, K., Press, O., and Narasimhan, K. “SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) (arXiv:2310.06770), 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770

Related Posts

  • Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B Bet on Self-Improving AI: the recursive-self-improvement bet this benchmark tests one rung down, where nine frontier models fully resolve zero tasks.
  • Agentic Coding Is a Trap: Lars Faye’s architectural-quality argument, for which ProgramBench supplies the numbers on monolithic single-file outputs and one-turn code dumps.
  • AutoCodeBench: Large Language Models are Automatic Code Benchmark Generators: another agent-built code benchmark where frontier models top out low, and a contrast in how the test suite is generated.
  • Overzealous Coding Models: a related failure of architectural judgment, models doing too much in one sweep rather than the disciplined edits a from-scratch rebuild needs.
  • How Claude Code Works in Large Codebases: Best Practices and Where to Start: the harness-side answer to from-scratch difficulty, the scaffolding that real coding agents lean on where ProgramBench strips it away.

item.title: Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B Bet on Self-Improving AI
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The New York Times reports that Recursive Superintelligence, a stealth-mode AI lab with offices in San Francisco and London, has emerged with more than $650 million in funding at a valuation above $4 billion. The investors include GV (formerly Google Ventures), Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD. Richard Socher, CEO of You.com and former head of AI research at Salesforce, founded the company with seven co-founders. NYT names four: Josh Tobin, Jeff Clune, and Tim Shi, all from OpenAI, plus Yuandong Tian from Meta. The six-month-old company has fewer than 30 employees, and has separately hired Peter Norvig, 25-year director of research at Google and co-author of Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, the standard university AI textbook for three decades. Long-term, the founders aim to apply the technology beyond AI itself, to drug discovery and biological research.

A.I. is code. And now, A.I. can code. The ingredients are there.

— Richard Socher

My Notes

  • Recursive self-improvement is becoming a funded category. Recursive Superintelligence joins a competitive field that already includes AMI Labs (world models; see Yann LeCun’s recent appearance for the thesis), Ineffable Intelligence (RL, David Silver’s), and Safe Superintelligence (safety-first), plus Mirendil and Anthropic’s Automated Alignment Researchers per Jack Clark’s Import AI 455. Add to the list Sakana AI, whose “AI Scientist” papers have been pushing automated research-paper production since 2024 and which Jack didn’t mention. NYT also notes a separately-funded namesake (Ricursive Intelligence, also valued at $4B, also chasing recursive self-improvement) and confirms Anthropic and OpenAI are pursuing the same outcome. The category is consolidating before its first public technical milestone.

  • The founders are an open-endedness team. NYT explicitly characterizes the team that way: “Many of these researchers specialize in a kind of AI development called ‘open-endedness.’ This involves building software systems that can run for days, months or even years in pursuit of goals set by the researchers.” Jeff Clune is the most public face of the lineage: POET, MAP-Elites, AI-generating algorithms, all arguing systems should generate their own training distribution. Yuandong Tian brings Meta’s RL/self-play track (OpenGo, Searchformer). Josh Tobin brings OpenAI robotics (domain randomization, Dactyl). Tim Shi (Cresta) is the agent-deployment hand. Peter Norvig gives the project the textbook-canonical AI brand.

  • OpenAI’s “automated AI researcher” is the concrete benchmark. Sam Altman said OpenAI hopes to have a system doing the work of a “less experienced” researcher by fall 2026. Recursive Superintelligence is pitching a years-long arc instead; Socher himself told NYT the technology will need years, and the article notes that “humans like Dr. Socher must still generate the new ideas that drive AI development forward.” The category’s strongest tension sits in that gap between a quarter-by-quarter benchmark and a years-long bet.

Related Posts

  • Are AI Systems About to Start Building Themselves?: Jack Clark’s read of the public evidence on automating AI R&D, the thesis this $4B bet is funding against.
  • AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions: an interview study of 25 researchers on the same automated-AI-development path, including the lab-versus-academia split this lab belongs to.
  • Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning: a position paper arguing genuine self-improvement needs the agent to design its own meta-loop, a sharper bar than the open-endedness lineage these founders bring.
  • ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?: a direct test of the rebuild-and-improve-your-own-systems capability this bet assumes, where frontier models fully resolve zero tasks.
  • AI Joins the Research Loop: the broader move of AI into open research that this lab aims to automate, with the recurring caveat that the trustworthy part is whatever can be checked.

item.title: Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models [1] (arXiv preprint, September 2025), Mark Steyvers, Catarina Belem, and Padhraic Smyth (UC Irvine) show that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on consistency-derived confidence targets raises both calibration and discrimination of verbalized LLM confidence (within domain, across new domains, and across two different metacognitive task formats), but only when the training data covers both formats jointly.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in decision-making contexts, but when they present answers without signaling low confidence, users may unknowingly act on erroneous outputs. Prior work shows that LLMs maintain internal uncertainty signals, yet their expressed confidence is often miscalibrated and poorly discriminates between correct and incorrect answers. We investigate whether supervised fine-tuning can improve models’ ability to communicate uncertainty and whether such improvements generalize across tasks and domains. We fine-tune LLMs on datasets spanning general knowledge, mathematics, and open-ended trivia, and evaluate two metacognitive tasks: (1) single-question confidence estimation, where the model assigns a numeric certainty to its answer, and (2) pairwise confidence comparison, where the model selects which of two answers it is more likely to answer correctly. We assess generalization to unseen domains, including medical and legal reasoning. Results show that fine-tuning improves calibration (alignment between stated confidence and accuracy) and discrimination (higher confidence for correct vs. incorrect responses) within and across domains. However, gains are task-specific: training on single-question calibration does not transfer to pairwise comparison, and vice versa. Multitask fine-tuning yields broader gains, lowering calibration error and strengthening discrimination in out-of-domain evaluations. This suggests that uncertainty communication in LLMs is trainable but requires multitask training to generalize effectively.

Methods

The authors define two metacognitive tasks that probe the same underlying ability — verbalizing internal uncertainty — through different output formats:

  • Single-question confidence (S) — the model emits an answer plus a numeric confidence (e.g. “my confidence is 0.75”). Scored with two metrics: Expected Calibration Error (ECE), the bin-weighted average gap between predicted confidence and empirical accuracy (11 bins of width 0.1), and Area Under the Curve (AUC), the probability that the model assigns higher confidence to a correct answer than to an incorrect one.
  • Pairwise confidence comparison (C) — given two questions, the model picks which one it is more likely to answer correctly. Scored with two AUC variants: AUC (does the selection match the question with the higher consistency-derived reference confidence?) and AUC (does the selection match which question the model actually answers correctly?).

Both formats are illustrated side-by-side in Figure 1.

Training labels are derived from the model’s own behavior, not human annotations. For each training question the authors sample the model multiple times, compute a consistency score across samples and the modal answer, then build two parallel training sets:

  • Single-question targets — each training question gets two targets: an answer target and a confidence target. The answer target is the modal answer — the answer that appears most often across the multiple samples drawn from the model. The confidence target comes from a calibration mapping that does use ground-truth correctness:
    • Across the labeled training-set questions, the authors compute consistency scores, bin questions by score, and record the empirical accuracy (fraction actually correct, using ground truth) in each bin — yielding a curve that maps consistency accuracy.
    • For each training question with consistency , the confidence target is (small noise added to prevent the model from memorizing the discrete bin boundaries) — i.e., “questions whose samples agree this much come out right this often, on average.”
  • Pairwise targets — each training example is a pair of questions and gets a single selection target: which of the two the model should claim higher confidence on. The supervision label is whichever question has the higher consistency score (the ranking is what matters here, so the raw consistency score is enough — no calibration-curve lookup needed).

The full pipeline — sample, score, look up calibrated target, build training set — is laid out in Figure 2.

They fine-tune two base models (GPT-4.1-mini via OpenAI’s SFT API and Llama-3.1-70B locally) under three training conditions — S (single-question targets only), C (pairwise targets only), or C+S (both jointly, the multitask condition) — on three within-domain corpora: MMLU-PRO (M), GSM8K (G), and TriviaQA (T), plus the M+G+T mixture. Held-out evaluation uses both within-domain test splits and three out-of-domain corpora: TruthfulQA, MetaMedQA, and LegalBench. Significance is assessed with a paired bootstrap over 1,000 resamples.

Results

Evaluation covers six datasets across two base models, two task formats (single-question S, pairwise C), three training conditions (S, C, C+S as defined above), and three generalization tiers (within-domain, across-domain, across-task). ECE measures calibration error (lower is better); AUC measures discrimination (higher is better). One thing to keep in mind for interpreting the deltas: the SFT loss never sees ground-truth answer labels directly — training tuples pair each question with the model’s own modal answer and a confidence scalar. Ground truth enters the pipeline only offline to fit the consistency-to-accuracy curve that produces those scalars. The recipe is therefore not aimed at improving factual accuracy, and Appendix Table A3 reports that accuracy is in fact similar before vs. after fine-tuning across all conditions. Pre/post deltas in ECE and AUC can therefore be read primarily as changes in confidence behavior, not in answer quality.

The cover figure (Figure 3) shows the within-domain calibration curves at a glance: baselines (cyan) sit below the diagonal, with confidence values clustered in [0.85, 0.95] but actual accuracy much lower at those points — overconfidence; the fine-tuned curves (pink) hug the diagonal across the full [0, 1] range. Table 1 quantifies the effect across all three generalization tiers.

The findings:

  • Within-domain SFT works on the trained format (Table 1 rows 1–6, Table 2 rows 1–6). On the format the model is trained on, ECE collapses and AUC lifts substantially across all three corpora. Multi-domain training (M+G+T) does not interfere with per-domain gains.
  • Cross-domain transfer holds for the trained format (rows 7–9). Single-task SFT trained on M+G+T improves both metrics on TruthfulQA, MetaMedQA, and LegalBench — except on TruthfulQA, where ECE actually rises because the baseline was already well-calibrated there.
  • Across-task transfer fails — and can backfire (rows 10–12). Pairwise-only SFT worsens single-question calibration on the already-calibrated domain and yields no AUC gain. Single-task SFT tested on the pairwise format shows the symmetric failure. Format isn’t a free transfer.
  • Multitask SFT (C+S) recovers and adds (rows 13–15). Joint training lifts AUC and drops ECE on the out-of-domain evaluations, beating single-task SFT alone — except again on TruthfulQA, where the already-calibrated-domain regression persists.
  • Llama-3.1-70B partially diverges. Single-question gains mirror GPT-4.1-mini, but multitask fine-tuning fails to lift Llama’s out-of-domain pairwise discrimination relative to comparison-only training. The “multitask helps both formats” headline is GPT-specific.

Figure 4 plots the OOD calibration curves under multitask SFT — the diagonal-hugging gain is largest on LegalBench, where the baseline was most overconfident.

My Notes

  • The “self-consistency only” framing is overstated: the paper says “the model is not trained using ground-truth correctness signals” (§2.1). True at the loss level: the SFT loss doesn’t reference per-question GT labels. But the confidence target depends on , the empirical accuracy at consistency , computed by comparing modal answers to ground truth (§4.3.2). The recipe inherits the label dependency of any supervised calibration method.

  • What this paper actually adds: consistency-based SFT is prior art (the authors cite three earlier works). The contribution is the 3×3×3 grid (training condition × generalization tier × test domain), which documents three failure modes: across-task transfer fails, well-calibrated domains regress under joint training, and Llama doesn’t inherit the multitask benefit on the comparison task. Does semantic entropy [2] or the verbal-confidence work in Kadavath et al. [3] have similar transfer failures? Their evaluations don’t run this grid.

  • S and C may be separable abilities: the paper concludes single-question (S) and pairwise (C) tasks are “distinct metacognitive routines, not interchangeable manifestations of a single uncertainty signal” (§2.3). The evidence: training only on S doesn’t improve C performance, and training only on C doesn’t improve S (Table 1 rows 10–12, Table 2 rows 10–12). Open question: is the underlying uncertainty signal also format-specific, or does the split only emerge at verbalization? AbstentionBench [4], metacognition atlas [5], and compliance-trap [6] each catalog one uncertainty failure mode (abstention, monitorability, prompt-regime collapse); this paper adds format-specific transfer. None has measured them together.

  • Calibration cost on already-calibrated domains: on TruthfulQA the baseline ECE is already 0.10; multitask SFT raises it to 0.13. A training intervention that helps most domains can hurt a well-behaved one. The Cacioli atlas [5] showed monitorability varies by 0.3+ AUC across MMLU subjects from the same base model; this paper adds that an SFT intervention’s sign can flip with domain. Evaluate the target domain’s pre-SFT calibration before deploying.

  • Compare to the test-time SVM harness: a recent metacognitive harness for Sonnet-4.6 [7] solves the same problem at the inference layer instead of via SFT. The harness leaves the model untouched and fits a small external SVM mapping , where FOK is the model’s pre-solve confidence rating and JOL is the post-solve rating. Inference flow: model emits FOK; if low, allocate more reasoning budget; model solves and emits JOL; SVM gives ; if , accept, else draw more attempts and aggregate. Both methods need GT correctness offline (this paper to fit , the harness to fit the SVM on a 100-question anchor set). Trade-off: the harness needs only ~100 labeled questions per base model and produces a tiny artifact but refits per model; this paper needs a larger labeled set and full SFT but produces a self-contained model that emits a calibrated confidence number from one sample at inference.

  • Practical alternative to abstention-from-prompting: the compliance-trap result [6] showed structural prompt constraints degrade frontier abstention by up to 30 accuracy points. This paper offers a weight-level analogue: train calibration into the model directly, so the prompt has less to override at inference. Follow-up: rerun compliance-trap on a model fine-tuned with this recipe; does the 8–30 point drop shrink?

References

  1. Steyvers, M., Belem, C., and Smyth, P. “Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2510.05126), September 30, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05126

  2. Farquhar, S., Kossen, J., Kuhn, L., and Gal, Y. “Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy.” Nature 630, pages 625–630 (arXiv:2406.15927), June 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15927

  3. Kadavath, S., Conerly, T., Askell, A., Henighan, T., Drain, D., Perez, E., Schiefer, N., Hatfield-Dodds, Z., DasSarma, N., Tran-Johnson, E., et al. “Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2207.05221), July 11, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221

  4. Kirichenko, P., Ibrahim, M., Chaudhuri, K., and Bell, S. J. “AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions.” NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (arXiv:2506.09038). https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038

  5. Cacioli, J.-P. “Domain-level metacognitive monitoring in frontier LLMs: A 33-model atlas.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.06673), April 21, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06673

  6. Kumar, R. “The Compliance Trap: How Structural Constraints Degrade Frontier AI Metacognition Under Adversarial Pressure.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.02398), May 14, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02398

  7. Cao, Q., Wang, Y., Qin, P., Zhang, S., and Xie, P. “LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.14186), May 13, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14186

Related Posts

  • Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback: the prompt-level analogue to this paper’s weight-level fix, eliciting calibrated verbal confidence without fine-tuning.
  • LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling: solves the same calibration problem at inference with an external SVM instead of SFT, the test-time counterpart contrasted in My Notes.
  • Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know: the foundational verbalized-confidence result this paper extends, showing models hold internal uncertainty signals that SFT can sharpen.
  • Domain-Level Metacognitive Monitoring in Frontier LLMs: A 33-Model Atlas: documents that calibration varies sharply by domain, reinforcing this paper’s finding that an SFT intervention’s sign can flip with the target domain.
  • A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses: unpacks the ECE and AUC metrics this paper reports, and what each one hides.
